one_line: Kai reviews Prism ML's Bonsai 2 (a 27B model compressed to about 1.75 bits per weight, 5.95 GB). The memory win is real, but the vendor's headline numbers hide reasoning-time, agentic and loader problems.
summary: The reviewer tests whether an 8 GB GPU can run a 27B model now that Prism ML's Bonsai 2 (a ternary, Hadamard-rotated quantization of Qwen 3.8 27B) ships at 5.95 GB versus 53.8 GB for FP16. He accepts the size and memory claim but argues the 98.2% retention headline is measured at maximum reasoning effort, against FP16 rather than the Q4 build most local users run. On the agentic benchmarks he cites (Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Verified) retention is about 75%, and the throughput column (TG128) is measured from a near-empty context, so real long-context speed is roughly half the headline or worse. He also warns that unofficial loaders (llama.cpp, Ollama, stock MLX) silently produce wrong output for this model and that only Prism ML's fork is correct. His verdict: stay on Q4 with 16 GB or more, and use Bonsai as the best chat and vision model that fits on 8 to 12 GB cards.
speakers: Kai (channel host, name not stated in transcript)

key_ideas.idea: The 9x size reduction is real: 27B at 5.95 GB versus 53.8 GB for FP16, so 8 to 12 GB cards can load a model class that previously needed two GPUs or a 64 GB Mac.
key_ideas.detail: Same 27.36B parameters, 262K context and Apache 2.0 license as the base Qwen 3.8 27B. The file-size claim is arithmetic, not marketing rounding.

key_ideas.idea: The compression uses ternary weights (-1, 0, +1) after a blockwise Hadamard rotation that spreads outliers, with one 16-bit scale per group of 128 weights.
key_ideas.detail: Lands at about 1.75 bits per weight as shipped. The rotation is what lets very low-bit rounding keep the signal.

key_ideas.idea: The 98.2% retention headline is against FP16, but the relevant baseline is the Q4 build most local users already run, and Q4 wins slightly.
key_ideas.detail: On the 14-benchmark thinking suite: FP16 averages 86.32, Bonsai 84.78, UDQ4 85.18 at about 17.6 GB. The reviewer says Q4 is the better choice if you have 16 GB or more.

key_ideas.idea: The headline score is measured at maximum reasoning effort. At medium effort retention drops to about 96%, and max reasoning multiplies generation time.
key_ideas.detail: Simon Willison's SVG pelican prompt at max reasoning used 22,276 reasoning tokens and 3,223 output tokens over 21 minutes, versus 3,715 output tokens in 137 seconds with reasoning off. Compression shrinks weights but not the thinking tokens.

key_ideas.idea: On agentic and engineering benchmarks retention is about 75%, not 98%. Independent testing also showed irreversible-action failures.
key_ideas.detail: Terminal Bench 2.1: 52.8 vs 69.7 (75.8%). SWE-bench Verified: 60.8 vs 80.6 (75.4%). One tester's 39 tool-use tests passed 9 of 13 modes. Reconciliation failed about 1 in 3 and irreversible actions about 2 in 3. In one run it deleted live rows without checking.

key_ideas.idea: The headline throughput uses TG128, which is measured from a near-empty context. Realistic agent contexts with a filling KV cache run much slower.
key_ideas.detail: Reported 129.9 tok/s on a 5090 and 47 tok/s on an M5 Max. At realistic lengths people saw teens to low 20s tok/s versus 40 to 60 for Q4. One debugging task took 27 minutes versus under 15 for Q4, and a time-zone bug went unfixed after over an hour.

key_ideas.idea: Bonsai 2 silently produces fluent, wrong output in llama.cpp, Ollama and stock MLX unless you use Prism ML's own fork (build B10658 or newer, as transcribed).
key_ideas.detail: Ollama's GGUF parser hits an unknown tensor type, returns size zero and continues. Stock MLX loaders skip the Hadamard transform without an error. An unofficial Ollama upload exists and gives convincing nonsense. The reviewer says to verify the build string before trusting any output.

key_ideas.idea: Context length dominates real VRAM. Normal chat at 4K context uses about 7.4 GB, but the full 262K window with a 4-bit KV cache needs about 12.9 GB.
key_ideas.detail: The VRAM figures are third-party measurements the reviewer cites on an 8 GB card. The advertised file size understates runtime memory.

key_ideas.idea: For 8 to 12 GB cards the comparison is different: Q4 does not fit, and the real alternatives are a 9B model or a 2-bit 27B build (IQ2) that scores 72.59 versus Bonsai's 84.78.
key_ideas.detail: Bonsai holds up on instruction following and vision tasks where the 2-bit build breaks. The reviewer's advice: use the best chat and vision model that fits, keep reasoning effort at default, not max.

techniques.name: Blockwise Hadamard rotation before ternary rounding
techniques.how: Multiply each weight block by a +1/-1 Hadamard matrix so outliers spread across the group. Then round to {-1, 0, +1} with one 16-bit scale per 128-weight group. This avoids outliers stretching the quantization range and crushing the middle values.
techniques.when: Low-bit (2-bit or ternary) weight quantization of LLMs where naive rounding loses signal to a few large-magnitude weights.

techniques.name: Compare compressed models against the baseline you actually run
techniques.how: Benchmark a quantized model against the Q4 (or whatever build you use) rather than the FP16 original. Check retention at the reasoning-effort setting you will run, and at realistic context lengths.
techniques.when: Evaluating a vendor's compression claim before choosing a model for a fixed VRAM budget.

techniques.name: Measure long-context generation speed, not TG128
techniques.how: Benchmark tokens/sec with the KV cache filled to your real agent prompt size (about 40K tokens or more), not from a near-empty context. Include the reasoning tokens in the time budget.
techniques.when: Sizing a local model for agentic coding workloads, where generation slows as the cache grows.

techniques.name: Verify local model loads before trusting output
techniques.how: Check the runtime build string and fork against the vendor's requirements. Run a known-answer prompt. Silent loader mismatches can produce fluent but wrong output.
techniques.when: Using a new quantization format that requires a custom fork or loader, especially when a community upload exists on a registry such as Ollama.

techniques.name: Keep reasoning effort at default for routine prompts
techniques.how: Leave reasoning effort at the model default and raise it only for hard prompts. Max effort can multiply generation time by an order of magnitude on slow hardware.
techniques.when: Running reasoning models on local hardware, or any token-metered setup where thinking tokens are the main cost.

techniques.name: Supported install path (as stated; repo name not given)
techniques.how: Clone the vendor's demo repo, run its setup command (the transcript says bonsai demo run setup), and start the server, which fetches the correct fork. Do not use an unofficial registry upload.
techniques.when: First-time setup of Bonsai 2 on a local GPU or Mac.

tools: Bonsai 2 (Prism ML 27B ternary model, 'Bonsai 227B' in auto-captions)
Ollama (GGUF parser; unofficial Bonsai upload on registry)
Prism ML fork (build B10658 or newer, as transcribed)
HumanEval Plus and LiveCodeBench (captioned as 'Human Evil Plus' and 'LifeCodeBench')

numbers.claim: Bonsai 2 file size 5.95 GB vs 53.8 GB FP16, about 9x smaller; Q4 build about 17.6 GB, about 3x larger than Bonsai
Quantization about 1.75 bits per weight; one 16-bit scale per 128-weight group
14-benchmark thinking average: FP16 86.32, Bonsai 84.78 (98.2% retention), UDQ4 85.18
Bonsai beats FP16 on AIME26 (95.83 vs 94.58) and IFBench (74 vs 71); the 1.54-point FP16 gap is within the noise of small test sets
Retention drops to about 96% at medium reasoning effort versus maximum
Pelican-on-bicycle prompt at max reasoning: 22,276 reasoning tokens, 3,223 output tokens, 21 minutes; reasoning off: 3,715 output tokens in 137 seconds
Estimated time to first useful token from 22,276 thinking tokens: about 245 s at 91.1 tok/s (RTX 4090), about 474 s at 47 tok/s (M5 Max)
Terminal Bench 2.1: 52.8 vs 69.7 FP16 (75.8% retained). SWE-bench Verified: 60.8 vs 80.6 (75.4% retained)
Independent tester: 9 of 13 tool-use modes perfect across 39 tests; reconciliation failed about 1 in 3, irreversible actions about 2 in 3
Throughput: TG128 129.9 tok/s on RTX 5090 and 47.0 tok/s on M5 Max; realistic long-context runs showed teens to low 20s tok/s versus 40 to 60 for Q4
Debugging task: Bonsai 27 minutes vs under 15 minutes for Q4
VRAM in use: about 7.4 GB at 4K context on an 8 GB card; about 12.9 GB at the full 262,144-token context with a 4-bit KV cache
Under 8 to 12 GB: IQ2 27B build scores 72.59 vs Bonsai 84.78, a 12.19-point lead at about two-thirds of the size

hot_takes: The headline 98% retention is a best-case number at max reasoning effort against FP16, not the Q4 build people run. The vendor's own table has Q4 slightly ahead.

On the agentic benchmarks that matter for coding agents, retention is about 75%, and the 'time' cost of reasoning tokens outweighs the memory win on 16 GB+ cards. Stay on Q4 if you have 16 GB or more.
Unofficial loaders (Ollama, llama.cpp, stock MLX) fail silently with this format and produce convincing wrong output. Bad reviews from those setups are likely and unfair to the compression itself.
For 8 to 12 GB cards the model is a real step up: the best chat and vision model that fits, beating the 2-bit alternatives by a wide margin.
Benchmark gaps of about 1.5 points are smaller than the noise of small test sets, so the vendor's 'beats the original' results should not be trusted.

relevance.why: InferCraft runs quantized models with KV-cache strategies on one RTX 5090. This review gives concrete evidence that TG128 overstates real agent-context speed, and that reasoning tokens dominate time on reasoning models.
relevance.action: Benchmark InferCraft quantization candidates at realistic KV-cache fill (about 40K tokens) and with reasoning tokens included in latency, not TG128 from a near-empty context. Add an agentic suite (Terminal Bench / SWE-bench-style tool tasks) to the correctness checks.

relevance.why: The reasoning-effort cost argument is relevant to cost-aware harness design, and the silent-failure point applies to any local fallback model, but the video does not cover harness workflows.
relevance.action: When a harness routes work to a local model, check the loader and build string against a known-answer test before trusting output, and budget reasoning effort per step.

relevance.why: Practitioner-grade warning that vendor compression benchmarks should be compared against the baseline you run, at the effort level you use, and that loader mismatches fail silently.
relevance.action: Before adopting a new quantized or local model, run the vendor's comparison against your own Q4 baseline, at your reasoning setting and context length, and check the runtime build string.
